q: What is the oxidation state of boron in borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O?
x: Water of crystallisation is neutral, so in Na₂B₄O₇: 2(+1) + 4x + 7(−2) = 0, giving 4x = 12 and x = +3. Forgetting the factor of 4 on boron or miscounting the oxygens gives +4 or +5.

q: Solid orthoboric acid, H₃BO₃, is soft, slippery and flaky. This is because in the crystal:
o: Planar B(OH)₃ units are joined by hydrogen bonds into layers, and the layers are held together only weakly
B³⁺ and OH⁻ ions form a strong ionic lattice
Boron and oxygen atoms form a three-dimensional giant covalent network
Boron atoms are held together by metallic bonding
x: In boric acid each planar B(OH)₃ unit is hydrogen-bonded to its neighbours within a sheet, and the sheets are held by weak forces, so they slide over each other like graphite. An ionic or giant covalent lattice would give a hard, high-melting solid, the most tempting slip.

q: Borax is used as a flux in soldering and brazing metals. When molten, borax cleans the metal surface because it:
o: Reduces the metal oxide film back to the metal
Covers the metal with a hard layer of boron nitride
Dissolves the metal oxide film, forming fusible metaborates
Lowers the melting point of the metal itself
x: Fused borax gives NaBO₂ and B₂O₃, and B₂O₃ combines with basic metal oxides to form low-melting metaborates, so the oxide layer is removed and the solder can wet the metal (the same chemistry as the borax bead). Thinking borax acts as a reducing agent is the usual slip.

q: Borax reacts with hydrochloric acid: Na₂B₄O₇ + 2HCl + 5H₂O → 2NaCl + 4H₃BO₃. What volume of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl reacts exactly with 3.82 g of borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O (molar mass 382 g mol⁻¹)?
x: 3.82 / 382 = 0.010 mol borax, which needs 2 × 0.010 = 0.020 mol HCl; volume = 0.020 / 0.20 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³. Ignoring the 1 : 2 mole ratio gives 50 cm³.

q: Which of the following double salts is NOT an alum?
x: Alums have the general formula M₂SO₄·M'₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, with a univalent and a trivalent cation (chrome alum, ferric alum and soda alum all fit). Mohr's salt, FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O, contains Fe²⁺ and only 6 waters, so it is a double salt but not an alum; ferric alum is tempting because it also contains iron.

q: 6.2 g of boric acid, H₃BO₃, is titrated with 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, glycerol being added to sharpen the end point. What volume of NaOH is needed? (H = 1, B = 11, O = 16)
x: M(H₃BO₃) = 3 + 11 + 48 = 62 g mol⁻¹, so 6.2 g = 0.10 mol. Boric acid is monobasic (it accepts OH⁻ to give [B(OH)₄]⁻), so 0.10 mol NaOH = 100 cm³. Treating it as tribasic because it has three H atoms gives 300 cm³.

q: 38.2 g of borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O (molar mass 382 g mol⁻¹), is heated strongly until it forms a clear glass of NaBO₂ and B₂O₃. What is the mass of the glass? (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
x: 0.10 mol borax loses 10 × 0.10 = 1.0 mol water (18.0 g), leaving 20.2 g of Na₂B₄O₇; the change Na₂B₄O₇ → 2NaBO₂ + B₂O₃ loses no mass, so the glass is 20.2 g. Giving the mass of water lost (18.0 g) instead of the residue is the most common slip.

q: Which statement about the hydroxides of boron and aluminium is correct?
o: Both are amphoteric, because both elements are in Group IIIA
B(OH)₃ is basic but Al(OH)₃ is acidic, because aluminium is the larger atom
B(OH)₃ is acidic but Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric, because boron is smaller with a higher ionisation energy and is non-metallic
Both are strongly basic, because both elements lose three electrons
x: Boron is a small, high-ionisation-energy non-metal, so B(OH)₃ behaves only as an acid; aluminium is more metallic, and Al(OH)₃ dissolves in both acids and alkalis. Assuming the same behaviour for the whole group is the tempting slip.

q: The basic structural unit present in all silicate minerals is:
x: Every silicate is built from SiO₄⁴⁻ tetrahedra, with silicon at the centre and four oxygen atoms at the corners, linked in different ways by sharing oxygens. SiO₃²⁻ is the repeating unit of chain silicates, not the basic unit.

q: White lead, once widely used as a white paint pigment, is:
x: White lead is basic lead carbonate, 2PbCO₃·Pb(OH)₂. Pb₃O₄ is red lead, PbCrO₄ is the yellow pigment chrome yellow, and PbO₂ is a dark brown oxide; red lead is the usual mix-up.

q: In making silicone oils, a little (CH₃)₃SiCl is mixed with (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ before hydrolysis. The role of the (CH₃)₃SiCl is to:
o: Form cross-links between chains, since it has three methyl groups
Stop chain growth, since it has only one Si–Cl bond and so caps the chain ends
Act as a catalyst for the condensation
Absorb the HCl formed during hydrolysis
x: (CH₃)₃SiCl hydrolyses to (CH₃)₃SiOH, which has only one OH and can condense at one end only, so it caps a chain and controls its length. Cross-linking needs three Si–Cl bonds on one silicon (CH₃SiCl₃); confusing three methyl groups with three Si–Cl bonds is the tempting slip.

q: Silicones are used to make fabrics and masonry water-repellent mainly because:
o: They react with water to form insoluble silica
Their Si–O bonds form hydrogen bonds with water and hold it
They are ionic solids that do not dissolve in water
Their non-polar alkyl groups face outward around the Si–O–Si backbone and repel water
x: A silicone has an Si–O–Si backbone with methyl (or other alkyl) groups on silicon; these hydrocarbon groups on the outside are non-polar, so water is not attracted and runs off. Silicones are covalent polymers and are chemically inert to water, so the hydrolysis option is wrong.

q: In a sheet silicate such as mica or talc, each SiO₄ tetrahedron shares three of its oxygen atoms with neighbouring tetrahedra. The empirical formula of the silicate anion is:
x: Each Si has one unshared O plus three shared O counted as half each: 1 + 3/2 = 5/2 O per Si, i.e. Si₂O₅; charge = 2(+4) + 5(−2) = −2. Sharing two oxygens (chains) gives SiO₃²⁻, the most tempting wrong option.

q: Lead(II) nitrate crystals are heated strongly in a dry tube. The products are:
x: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂; brown NO₂ is seen and yellow PbO is left. Only nitrates such as NaNO₃ and KNO₃ stop at the nitrite and oxygen, which is the tempting slip; Pb(+2) is the stable state, so PbO₂ does not form.

q: In a fully charged lead-acid storage battery, the active material of the positive plate and the oxidation state of lead in it are:
x: The positive plate carries lead(IV) oxide, PbO₂ (Pb +4), and the negative plate spongy lead; on discharge both turn into PbSO₄. Choosing PbSO₄ describes a discharged plate, the usual slip.
